newsitem.title: USA: Disease found to attack both sexes equally - study.
newsitem.headline: Disease found to attack both sexes equally - study.

text.p: Chlamydia, one of the world's most common sexually transmitted infections, was no more likely to strike women than men, a study said on Tuesday, running counter to previous research.

Researchers at the National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases said they based that conclusion on a study of 494 couples in the Baltimore area who were treated at sexually transmitted disease clinics.
Previous studies had uncovered what appeared to be higher infection rates among female partners of infected males than among men whose female partners were infected.

About 50 million new cases of chlamydial infection occur around the world each year. The bacteria causes a number of health problems including urethral inflammation in men and pelvic inflammatory disease in women, a condition that can lead to infertility and tubal pregnancies.

The study, in this week's Journal of the American Medical Association, suggested that previous tests were not sensitive enough to pick up equal levels of infection among both sexes. "The high prevalance of infection ... underscores the need for routine testing for both males and females for genital chlamydia infections," the study concluded.
